---
title: "Session 3: Data manipulation (dplyr, tidyr, joins)"
subtitle: "dplyr, tidyr and joins: from a raw table to the table you need"
---

::: {.objectifs}
Session objectives

- Chain operations with the pipe `|>` and use the main `dplyr` verbs: `filter`, `select`, `arrange`, `mutate`, `rename`, `summarise`.
- Create variables with `case_when()` and `if_else()`; order categories with factors.
- Handle missing values explicitly and always report the number of observations (N).
- Reshape a table between wide and long format with `tidyr`.
- Combine tables with joins, and detect a join that silently loses observations.

:::

::: {.prepare}
Prepare your R session

**Packages used today:** `tidyverse`, `here`. If one is missing: `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here"))`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en")   # R messages in English
library(tidyverse)   # dplyr, tidyr, forcats, ggplot2, readr...
library(here)
source(here("R", "theme_cours.R"))

wdi <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
# CAF life expectancy is unreliable in this WDI release (14.7 in 2009, 18.8 in 2022): exclude every year
wdi <- wdi |> mutate(life_exp = if_else(iso3c == "CAF", NA_real_, life_exp))
```

**Script of this session:** [download seance-3.R](../scripts/seance-3.R){download="seance-3.R"}, all the code of this page in one file.
:::

The question that runs through the course: **"Growth, health and inequality: what do the data say about developing countries?"** Today we use the World Bank panel (all countries, 2000-2023) and learn to cut it into the pieces we need.

```{r}
glimpse(wdi)
```

Each row is a country-year: `r n_distinct(wdi$iso3c)` countries, `r n_distinct(wdi$year)` years, `r nb(nrow(wdi), 0)` rows.

The setup already applies one correction: the life expectancy of the Central African Republic (`CAF`) is set to missing (`NA`) for every year, because this release of the series is unreliable (Session 4 shows it). So the summaries of `life_exp` below use `na.rm = TRUE`, which skips missing values; we explain it in the section on missing values.

## The pipe and the main verbs

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 35 min]{.duration} After this section you can write a chain of `dplyr` verbs that filters, selects, sorts and creates variables.
:::

### The pipe `|>`

The pipe takes what is on its left and passes it as the **first argument** of the function on its right. Read it as "and then".

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  A[wdi] --> B["filter(year == 2020)"]
  B --> C["select(country, life_exp)"]
  C --> D["arrange(desc(life_exp))"]
  D --> E[Result table]
```

::: {.definition}
**Pipe (`|>`)**: an operator that sends the result on its left into the first argument of the function on its right. `x |> f(y)` is the same as `f(x, y)`.
:::

```{r}
# Without the pipe: read from the inside out
head(arrange(filter(wdi, year == 2020), desc(life_exp)), 3)

# With the pipe: read from top to bottom
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  arrange(desc(life_exp)) |>
  head(3)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Every `dplyr` verb takes a table and returns a table. That is why they chain: **one verb per line, read top to bottom as "and then"**.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Older code online uses the `%>%` pipe from the `magrittr` package. It does almost the same thing. Both work; in this course we use the native `|>`.
:::

### `filter()`: keep rows

`filter()` keeps the **rows** where the condition is `TRUE`. Several conditions separated by a comma mean "and"; use `|` for "or" and `%in%` for "one of".

```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020, region == "South Asia") |>
  select(country, life_exp, gdp_pc_ppp)

wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020, iso3c %in% c("FRA", "DEU", "ESP")) |>
  select(country, life_exp)
```

Comparison operators: `==` (equal; **never a single `=`**), `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`.

### `select()`: keep columns

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Confusing the two: `filter()` works on **rows** (conditions on values), `select()` works on **columns** (names). If R says "object not found" inside `filter()`, check that you did not drop the column with an earlier `select()`.
:::

```{r}
wdi |> select(country, year, life_exp) |> head(3)

# Helpers: select columns by pattern or by type
wdi |> select(country, starts_with("gdp")) |> head(3)
wdi |> select(contains("_")) |> head(3)
wdi |> select(where(is.numeric)) |> names()
```

`select(-gini)` drops a column. `select()` can also reorder: `select(iso3c, country, everything())`.

### `arrange()`: sort rows

```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  arrange(desc(gdp_pc_ppp)) |>   # desc() = largest first
  select(country, gdp_pc_ppp) |>
  head(5)
```

### `mutate()` and `rename()`: create and rename columns

```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  mutate(gdp_bn = gdp / 1e9,                      # GDP in billions of US$
         pop_m  = population / 1e6) |>            # population in millions
  select(country, gdp_bn, pop_m) |>
  arrange(desc(gdp_bn)) |>
  head(3)
```

`rename(new_name = old_name)` changes a column name:

```{r}
wdi |> rename(life_expectancy = life_exp) |> names()
```

### `if_else()` and `case_when()`: conditional variables

`if_else(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)` handles two cases; `case_when()` handles as many as you want. Conditions are tested **in order**; the first `TRUE` wins; `.default` catches the rest.

```{r}
wdi_2020 <- wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  mutate(
    high_life = if_else(life_exp >= 75, "75+ years", "under 75"),
    elec_level = case_when(
      elec_access >= 99 ~ "universal (99%+)",
      elec_access >= 80 ~ "high (80-99%)",
      elec_access >= 50 ~ "medium (50-80%)",
      elec_access <  50 ~ "low (<50%)",
      .default = "no data"
    )
  )

wdi_2020 |> count(elec_level)
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of the number of countries in each electricity-access level in 2020. The longest bar is the highest level: most countries have near-universal access."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the chart code (taught in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
wdi_2020 |>
  count(elec_level) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(elec_level, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_cours[["principal"]]) +
  labs(title = "Most countries have near-universal electricity access",
       x = "Number of countries, 2020", y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2020.")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## In plain words
`case_when()` is a sorting machine: each country goes through the questions from top to bottom and **stops at the first "yes"**. That is why the order of the conditions matters.
:::

`count()` is a shortcut for "group and count the rows". We come back to it below.

## Summarising by group, and missing values

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 30 min]{.duration} After this section you can compute a statistic by group, and say how many observations it rests on.
:::

### `group_by()` + `summarise()`

`summarise()` collapses many rows into one. Combined with `group_by()` it gives **one row per group**. `n()` counts the rows of each group.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  A["wdi, 2020 (one row per country)"] --> B["group_by(region)"]
  B --> C["summarise(mean_life = mean(life_exp))"]
  C --> D["one row per region"]
```

```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(
    n_countries = n(),
    median_life = median(life_exp, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_gdp_pc = median(gdp_pc_ppp)
  )
```

Here is the same logic with the mean, saved so that we can plot it:

```{r}
life_by_region <- wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(mean_life = mean(life_exp, na.rm = TRUE), n_countries = sum(!is.na(life_exp)))

life_by_region
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars of mean life expectancy at birth in 2020 for each world region, sorted, with the number of countries labelled on each bar. Sub-Saharan Africa has the shortest bar, North America among the longest."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the chart code (taught in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
life_by_region |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_life, y = fct_reorder(region, mean_life))) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_cours[["principal"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n_countries)), hjust = 1.1, colour = "white") +
  labs(title = str_wrap("Sub-Saharan Africa trails North America by 17 years", 60),
       x = "Mean life expectancy at birth, 2020 (years)", y = NULL,
       caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2020. Unweighted mean across countries.", 95))
```

Now look at `median_gdp_pc` in the previous table: `NA` for five of the seven regions. One missing value is enough for `median()` to return `NA`. We need to talk about missing values.

### Missing values

`NA` means "value unknown". It is **contagious**: any calculation involving an `NA` returns `NA`.

```{r}
mean(c(70, 75, NA))
mean(c(70, 75, NA), na.rm = TRUE)   # ignore the NAs
```

How many `NA` per column in our panel?

```{r}
wdi |> summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x))))
```

`gini` is missing for `r nb_pct(100 * mean(is.na(wdi$gini)))` of the country-years: inequality is measured by household surveys, which are not run every year. Three tools:

- `is.na(x)` returns `TRUE` where `x` is missing. Use it inside `filter()`.
- `drop_na(var)` removes the rows where `var` is missing (without argument: any variable).
- `na.rm = TRUE` inside `mean()`, `median()`, `sum()`... ignores the `NA` in the calculation.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Removing NAs changes your N, and possibly your conclusion
Dropping missing values is **not neutral**: the countries that have no Gini are not a random sample (they are often poorer or less well covered by statistics). Always report how many observations each number rests on.
:::

```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  summarise(
    n_countries   = n(),
    n_with_gdp_pc = sum(!is.na(gdp_pc_ppp)),
    n_with_gini   = sum(!is.na(gini)),
    median_gdp_pc = median(gdp_pc_ppp, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_gini   = median(gini, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

The median Gini is computed on **`n_with_gini` countries only**, not on all of them. Now the grouped table again, this time with N:

```{r}
gdp_n_region <- wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(
    n_countries   = n(),
    n_gdp_pc      = sum(!is.na(gdp_pc_ppp)),
    median_gdp_pc = median(gdp_pc_ppp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_gdp_pc))

gdp_n_region
```

Dropping the `NA` is not free. The chart shows how many countries each region loses:

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Stacked horizontal bars showing, for each region, the number of countries with GDP per capita kept and lost to missing values in 2020. The share lost differs widely across regions."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the chart code (taught in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
gdp_n_region |>
  mutate(lost = n_countries - n_gdp_pc) |>
  select(region, `Kept` = n_gdp_pc, `Lost (NA)` = lost) |>
  pivot_longer(-region, names_to = "status", values_to = "countries") |>
  mutate(status = factor(status, levels = c("Lost (NA)", "Kept"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = countries, y = fct_reorder(region, countries, sum), fill = status)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Kept = pal_cours[["principal"]], `Lost (NA)` = pal_cours[["accent"]]),
                    labels = c(Kept = "Kept", `Lost (NA)` = "Lost (NA)")) +
  labs(title = "Dropping NAs removes countries unevenly across regions",
       x = "Number of countries, 2020", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2020. GDP per capita (PPP).") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
`na.rm = TRUE` makes the calculation run, but **the statistic now describes a smaller, possibly different group of countries**. Print N next to every number.
:::

Two details. `.groups = "drop"` removes the grouping from the result (otherwise it stays grouped, which can surprise you later). And since dplyr 1.1, `.by` is a shorter alternative to `group_by()`, with no grouping left behind:

```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  summarise(mean_life = mean(life_exp, na.rm = TRUE), n = n(), .by = income)
```

`count()` is the quickest way to tabulate a categorical variable (`sort = TRUE` puts the largest first):

```{r}
wdi |> filter(year == 2020) |> count(income, sort = TRUE)
```

## Factors: giving categories an order

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 10 min]{.duration} After this section you can control the order in which categories appear in tables and charts.
:::

R sorts text alphabetically, which is rarely what we want. Income groups have a natural order. Note that `income` is the World Bank's **current** classification, applied to every year: a country that has changed group since 2000 appears in its present-day group even in 2000.

::: {.definition}
**Factor**: a variable with a fixed, ordered list of allowed categories (its `levels`). The order of the levels is the order used in tables and charts.
:::

```{r}
unique(wdi$income)   # check the exact labels before using them

income_levels <- c("Low income", "Lower middle income",
                   "Upper middle income", "High income")

wdi <- wdi |>
  mutate(income = factor(income, levels = income_levels))

wdi |> filter(year == 2020) |> count(income)
```

Now the table follows the economic order and not the alphabet. Other tools from `forcats` (loaded with `tidyverse`):

- `fct_relevel(x, "High income")` moves one level to the front without retyping all of them.
- `fct_reorder(x, y)` orders the levels of `x` by the values of `y`. This is what makes bar charts readable (Session 5).

*Preview: `ggplot` is taught in Session 5. For now, just copy the pattern.*

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars of median life expectancy at birth in 2020 for each region, sorted from shortest to longest. Sub-Saharan Africa has the shortest bar."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  summarise(median_life = median(life_exp, na.rm = TRUE), .by = region) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = median_life, y = fct_reorder(region, median_life))) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_cours[["principal"]]) +
  labs(title = str_wrap("Life expectancy is lowest in Sub-Saharan Africa", 60),
       x = "Median life expectancy at birth, 2020 (years)",
       y = NULL,
       caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, WDI. Median across countries of each region.", 95))
```

Without `fct_reorder()`, the bars would be in alphabetical order and the message would be harder to read.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Typing a level with a slightly different spelling (`"Low Income"` instead of `"Low income"`): **R silently turns it into `NA`**. That is why we ran `unique(wdi$income)` first. After `factor()`, check with `count()` that no `NA` appeared.
:::

## Reshaping with tidyr: wide and long

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can switch a table between wide and long format with `pivot_wider()` and `pivot_longer()`.
:::

### Tidy data in three rules

::: {.definition}
**Tidy data**: a table is tidy when (1) each **variable** is a column, (2) each **observation** is a row, (3) each **value** is a cell.
:::

Our panel is tidy: one row per country-year, one column per variable (`year` is a column, not 24 columns). `ggplot2` and `dplyr` expect this *long* format.

But data downloaded from the World Bank website or an Excel sheet usually come *wide*: one column per year (`2000`, `2001`, ...). It is handy to read, but a year is a value, not a variable. Before analysing such data, you reshape them.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  L["Long: one row per country-year"] -- "pivot_wider()" --> W["Wide: one column per year"]
  W -- "pivot_longer()" --> L
```

:::: {layout-ncol=2}
::: {}
**Long** (3 columns)

| country | year | value |
|---------|------|-------|
| A | 2000 | 70 |
| A | 2010 | 73 |
| B | 2000 | 55 |
| B | 2010 | 60 |
:::

::: {}
**Wide** (one column per year)

| country | y2000 | y2010 |
|---------|-------|-------|
| A | 70 | 73 |
| B | 55 | 60 |
:::
::::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Ask: "is this column name actually a **value**?" Column names `2000`, `2010`, ... are values of the variable `year`: pivot them into rows with `pivot_longer()`.
:::

### `pivot_wider()`: long to wide

Life expectancy for five countries, one column per year:

```{r}
life_long <- wdi |>
  filter(country %in% c("Algeria", "Brazil", "Ghana", "India", "Norway"),
         year %in% c(2000, 2010, 2020)) |>
  select(country, year, life_exp)

life_long

life_wide <- life_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = life_exp, names_prefix = "y")

life_wide
```

**`names_from`** gives the column that becomes the new column names, `values_from` the column that fills the cells.

### `pivot_longer()`: wide to long

The way back, which is the one you will use most with Excel-style downloads:

```{r}
life_back <- life_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("y"),
               names_to = "year", names_prefix = "y",
               values_to = "life_exp") |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year))   # year came back as text

life_back

# Check: we recover exactly the table we started from
all.equal(as.data.frame(life_back), as.data.frame(life_long))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
After `pivot_longer()` with `names_prefix`, the new `year` column is **text**, not a number. Charts and filters on it then misbehave. Convert it with `as.integer()`, as above.
:::

## Joins: combining two tables

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 35 min]{.duration} After this section you can combine two tables safely and detect rows that failed to match.
:::

Real projects use several sources: GDP from the World Bank, inequality from WID, trade from the OECD.

::: {.definition}
**Join**: adds to table `x` the columns of table `y`, matching rows on a **key**.
**Key**: the column (or columns) that identify the same unit in both tables, here the country code and the year.
:::

### A tiny example

```{r}
data1 <- tibble(country = c("US", "CN", "IN"), value1 = 1:3)
data2 <- tibble(country = c("US", "CN", "BR"), value2 = 4:6)

data1
data2
```

"US" and "CN" are in both tables, "IN" only on the left, "BR" only on the right. The four main joins differ in **which rows they keep**:

```{r}
left_join(data1, data2, by = "country")    # all rows of data1
inner_join(data1, data2, by = "country")   # only rows found in both
full_join(data1, data2, by = "country")    # all rows of both
anti_join(data1, data2, by = "country")    # rows of data1 with NO match in data2
```

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  subgraph X["x: US, CN, IN"]
    x1[US]
    x2[CN]
    x3[IN]
  end
  subgraph Y["y: US, CN, BR"]
    y1[US]
    y2[CN]
    y3[BR]
  end
  X --> L["left_join keeps US, CN, IN"]
  X --> I["inner_join keeps US, CN"]
  X --> A["anti_join keeps IN"]
  Y --> I
```

| Join | Keeps | Rows here | Unmatched values |
|------------------|--------------------------|------|----------------------|
| `left_join(x, y)` | all rows of `x` | 3 (US, CN, IN) | `NA` for `y`'s columns |
| `inner_join(x, y)` | rows present in both | 2 (US, CN) | none |
| `full_join(x, y)` | all rows of both | 4 (US, CN, IN, BR) | `NA` on either side |
| `anti_join(x, y)` | rows of `x` absent from `y` | 1 (IN) | no `y` columns at all |

(`right_join(x, y)` is `left_join(y, x)` with the columns in another order; you can ignore it.)

`left_join()` is the default choice: you start from your main table and *add* information, without ever losing a row of the main table. `anti_join()` is not a way to merge but a **diagnostic**: it lists the keys that failed to match.

### The real-world trap: joining on country names

We want to add inequality data from the World Inequality Database (WID) to GDP from the World Bank, for three countries.

```{r}
gdp3 <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_3countries.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
wid  <- read_csv(here("data", "wid_gini.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# first row of each country
gdp3 |> arrange(country, year) |> distinct(country, .keep_all = TRUE)
wid  |> arrange(country_wid, year) |> distinct(country_wid, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

The natural idea: both tables have a country column, so join on it. (WID calls it `country_wid`, so we tell `by` that the two names are equivalent.)

```{r}
naive <- gdp3 |>
  left_join(wid, by = c("country" = "country_wid", "year"))

nrow(gdp3)
nrow(naive)

naive |>
  summarise(n_rows = n(), n_gini = sum(!is.na(gini)), .by = country)
```

No error, no warning, the right number of rows. And yet **the United States has no Gini at all**:

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars of the number of years, 2000-2020, with a Gini found or missing for each country after the join on names. The United States has only missing values."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the chart code (taught in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
naive |>
  summarise(n_gini = sum(!is.na(gini)), n_missing = sum(is.na(gini)), .by = country) |>
  pivot_longer(c(n_gini, n_missing), names_to = "status", values_to = "years") |>
  mutate(status = recode(status, n_gini = "Gini found", n_missing = "Gini missing (NA)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = years, y = country, fill = status)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Gini found` = pal_cours[["principal"]],
                               `Gini missing (NA)` = pal_cours[["accent"]]),
                    labels = c(`Gini found` = "Gini found", `Gini missing (NA)` = "Gini missing (NA)")) +
  labs(title = "The join on names silently lost the United States",
       x = "Number of years (2000-2020)", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Source: World Bank WDI and World Inequality Database (WID).") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Why? WDI writes "United States", WID writes "USA": the two strings differ, so no row matches, and `left_join()` fills with `NA`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Joining two sources by country name: the US silently loses its Gini and nobody notices, because R raises nothing. A join never complains about unmatched keys. **You** must check.
:::

Two checks that would have caught it:

```{r}
# 1. anti_join: which keys of the left table have no match on the right?
gdp3 |>
  anti_join(wid, by = c("country" = "country_wid", "year")) |>
  distinct(country)

# 2. count the NAs created by the join
sum(is.na(naive$gini))
```

The fix: **join on a standardised code, not on a name.** The ISO 3-letter code (`iso3c`) is the same in both sources. Names change ("Turkey" / "Turkiye", "Korea, Rep." / "South Korea"); codes are far more stable. They still change now and then (Romania went from ROM to ROU, DR Congo from ZAR to COD), so run `anti_join()` anyway.

```{r}
gdp_gini <- gdp3 |>
  left_join(select(wid, iso3c, year, gini), by = c("iso3c", "year"))

nrow(gdp3)
nrow(gdp_gini)
sum(is.na(gdp_gini$gini))

gdp_gini |>
  summarise(n_rows = n(), n_gini = sum(!is.na(gini)), .by = country)

# And the anti_join check is now empty
gdp3 |> anti_join(wid, by = c("iso3c", "year")) |> nrow()
```

We selected only `iso3c`, `year` and `gini` from `wid`: otherwise `country` and `country_wid` would both be carried along, which is confusing.

Now all three countries have a Gini, and we can finally compare inequality with income:

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the Gini coefficient by year for China, India and the United States. All three lines rise over the period; China's rise comes mostly before 2010."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the chart code (taught in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
gdp_gini |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = gini, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(China = pal_cours[["accent"]],
                                 India = "#E69F00",
                                 `United States` = pal_cours[["principal"]])) +
  labs(title = str_wrap("Inequality rose in all three countries; in China, mostly before 2010", 60),
       x = "Year", y = "Gini coefficient (WID, 0-1)",
       colour = NULL,
       caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank WDI (GDP) joined with World Inequality Database (WID, Gini) on iso3c and year.", 95))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Two Ginis that are not comparable
The `gini` column of `wdi` and the Gini of `wid` do not measure the same thing:

- **WDI** (0-100): household surveys, often of **consumption** rather than income in low- and middle-income countries, India included.
- **WID** (0-1): **pre-tax national income** among adults, combining surveys, tax records and national accounts.

They even rank India differently. In WID, India is the most unequal of the three countries in 2020 (0.63, against 0.62 for the United States and 0.56 for China). In WDI, India's latest Gini (23.0 in 2023) is far below that of the United States (41.8 in 2023). Never put the two in the same column or compare one with the other.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Why it matters for development economics
Cross-country work always combines sources (growth from the World Bank, inequality from WID, trade from the OECD). A silent loss like the US here biases every comparison that follows, usually **without any visible symptom**.
:::

### Good habits for every join

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
A join never complains about unmatched keys. The safety net is a routine: **join on codes, count rows, run `anti_join()`**.
:::

1. **Join on codes** (`iso3c`, not names), and on all the keys that identify a row: country *and* year here.
2. **Count rows before and after** with `nrow()`. After a `left_join()`, the number of rows should equal that of the left table.
3. **Run `anti_join()`** in both directions to see what did not match.
4. **Count the `NA`** in the new columns.

What if the key is not unique in the right table? For instance, joining on `iso3c` alone when `wid` has 21 years per country: each row of `gdp3` matches 21 rows of `wid`, and the result explodes to many more rows. Since dplyr 1.1, `*_join()` warns about unexpected many-to-many matches, and you can state your expectation with the `relationship` argument:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Each (iso3c, year) must appear at most once in wid, otherwise: error
gdp3 |>
  left_join(wid, by = c("iso3c", "year"), relationship = "many-to-one")
```

Do not ignore that warning: it almost always means the key is incomplete (here, `year` was forgotten).

## Exercises (≈ 45 min)

The following exercises use the panel `wdi`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 3.1: filter, select, arrange
Take the Sub-Saharan African countries in 2020. Keep `country`, `income`, `life_exp` and `elec_access`, and sort them by life expectancy, lowest first. Show the 10 lowest. How many countries are in the group?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
ssa_2020 <- wdi |>
  filter(region == "Sub-Saharan Africa", year == 2020) |>
  select(country, income, life_exp, elec_access) |>
  arrange(life_exp)

nrow(ssa_2020)   # N
head(ssa_2020, 10)
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 3.2: mutate
Add the column `gdp_bn` (GDP in billions of US$) to the 2020 data and list the 5 countries with the largest GDP, with their GDP in billions. Which of them are *not* high income?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  mutate(gdp_bn = gdp / 1e9) |>
  arrange(desc(gdp_bn)) |>
  select(country, income, gdp_bn) |>
  head(5)
```
The list contains China, which is not classified as high income by the World Bank.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 3.3: group_by and summarise
For each region **and** each year in 2000, 2010 and 2020, compute the median GDP per capita (PPP) and the number of countries it is based on (excluding missing values). Present the result sorted by year, then by median.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
wdi |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2010, 2020)) |>
  summarise(
    n_countries   = sum(!is.na(gdp_pc_ppp)),
    median_gdp_pc = median(gdp_pc_ppp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(region, year)
  ) |>
  arrange(year, desc(median_gdp_pc))
```
The N is not constant across regions and years: compare the medians with that in mind.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 3.4: pivot
Build a table with one row per region and one column per year (2000, 2010, 2020) containing the median life expectancy. Then bring it back to long format.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
life_region <- wdi |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2010, 2020)) |>
  summarise(median_life = median(life_exp, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(region, year)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = median_life, names_prefix = "y")

life_region

life_region |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("y"), names_to = "year", names_prefix = "y",
               values_to = "median_life") |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year))   # year comes back as text
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 3.5: join and check
Using `wdi`, build the table `elec` with `iso3c`, `year`, `elec_access` for 2020. Then join it to a table `small` that contains `iso3c = c("FRA", "GHA", "XXX")` (the last code does not exist). Use `left_join()`, check the number of rows, then use `anti_join()` to find the code that did not match.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
elec <- wdi |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  select(iso3c, year, elec_access)

small <- tibble(iso3c = c("FRA", "GHA", "XXX"))

joined <- small |> left_join(elec, by = "iso3c")

nrow(small)
nrow(joined)   # same: left_join keeps all rows of `small`
joined         # XXX has NA

small |> anti_join(elec, by = "iso3c")   # the code that failed to match
```
:::

## Key takeaways

- The pipe `|>` reads as "and then": one verb per line, top to bottom.
- `filter()` selects rows, `select()` columns, `arrange()` sorts, `mutate()` creates variables, `summarise()` (with `group_by()` or `.by`) collapses to one row per group.
- Missing values are contagious: `na.rm = TRUE` or `drop_na()` fix the calculation but change N. **Always report N.**
- Factors give categories a meaningful order (`factor(levels = )`, `fct_relevel()`, `fct_reorder()`).
- Tidy data: one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell. `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()` switch between formats.
- A join never complains about keys that do not match. Join on codes (`iso3c`), count rows before and after, and run `anti_join()`.
